title: Wildlife, Vertebrate Damage, and Exclusion
objective: Identify vertebrate damage from evidence and select lawful exclusion measures that do not create new crop, worker, or ecological hazards.
coreScience: Wildlife injury can include browsing, broken branches, stem girdling, digging, root disturbance, burrows, contamination, and irrigation damage. The same symptom can have several causes: clipped leaves may reflect deer, rabbits, rodents, insects, tools, or wind. Identification should use tracks, droppings, bite pattern, height, camera records, timing, and spatial distribution.

Exclusion is usually more reliable than repeated harassment, but it must match the animal and site. Fence height, mesh size, bottom sealing, gates, corners, soil contact, climbing surfaces, and maintenance determine performance. Bird netting can trap wildlife and workers if poorly installed. Electric fencing, traps, repellents, and wildlife handling are regulated and require lawful, labeled, and humane use.

Vegetation, mulch, debris, water, cover crops, and structures can provide habitat. Removing all habitat can harm beneficial species and erosion control, while uncontrolled habitat beside the crop can increase pressure. Management should separate crop protection from broader ecological goals.
cultivationRelevance: Use evidence to identify the likely animal, install preventive exclusion before crop value rises, inspect the entire perimeter, and record non-target impacts.
measureAndRecord: Before evaluating wildlife, vertebrate damage, and exclusion, record the site, crop, and measurement context, including Damage type/height/distribution, tracks/droppings/camera, species confidence, time. Use fixed locations, definitions, and instruments so later comparisons are not confounded by changing observation methods.

During the observation period, track crop stage, attractants and habitat, fence/net specification, gate and ground gaps together with date and time, weather or structure state, crop stage, and any intervention that could change the response. Preserve raw measurements and notable spatial variation rather than only summary values.

At the decision point, document inspection, repair, non-target injury, lawful authority.. Compare the result with the production objective, note uncertainty and exceptions, and retain enough traceability to reconstruct why the action was taken.
misconceptions: All missing leaves are deer damage. This is too simple because outdoor crop response also depends on genotype, developmental stage, local microclimate, soil or root-zone condition, and the way the variable was measured.

A taller fence fixes every wildlife problem. A single observation cannot establish the mechanism or predict the whole block; use representative locations, repeated measurements, and crop-response data before generalizing.
Repellents work indefinitely without adaptation. The statement should not be treated as a universal rule across sites, seasons, structures, cultivars, or management systems without local validation.
evidenceLimits: Wildlife laws, species behavior, migration, pressure, terrain, and structure design vary locally. Numerical thresholds and response magnitudes should therefore be treated as context-specific unless the cited evidence matches the site, cultivar, developmental stage, measurement method, and production system under review.

Climate normals, extension guidance, engineering references, and non-cannabis crop studies can support mechanism and planning, but they do not establish a universal cannabis target. Current local weather, site measurements, structural limits, and applicable rules remain required controls.
